caustica.options.rt.advancedGrading.tool: Off - the default - uses the authored look: the look package's scene-referred LMT followed by the ACES 2.0 display transform, which is also where the Look Transform control applies. On replaces both with the built-in AgX grading, which holds saturated colors vivid as highlights roll off and uses its own exposure and saturation sliders instead.
caustica.options.rt.exposureMode.tooltip: How the ray-traced image is mapped to display brightness. Auto adapts to scene luminance; Manual uses the exposure value directly.
caustica.options.rt.manualEv.tooltip: Exposure compensation in stops. In Manual, this is the fixed exposure. In Auto, this biases the auto exposure brighter or darker.
caustica.options.rt.nightLift.tooltip: How far night is moved off where auto exposure would place it, in stops. Negative is darker, positive is brighter, and 0.00 is the authored night. It follows how dark the sky is rather than how bright the frame looks, so a night scene holding a lantern or a lit window moves with it, and midday is untouched. Auto exposure sets one level for the whole image, so this darkens or brightens everything in the frame together, lamps included.
caustica.options.rt.rrEnabled.tooltip: Terminate dim indirect paths probabilistically instead of tracing them to the bounce cap. Much faster with near-identical results. Turning it off gives an unbiased, noisier estimator for A/B comparisons.
caustica.options.rt.cloudOutScatter.tool: Render the cloud deck in front of surfaces, not just in front of the sky. A ray that crosses the layer picks up the cloud's own scattered light and has everything behind it dimmed by Beer-Lambert extinction, so clouds veil the ground seen from above the deck and show up in reflections and refractions that land on terrain. Off leaves clouds a sky-only effect.
caustica.options.rt.gamma.tooltip: Final luminance gamma. Values below 1.00 brighten shadows and midtones while preserving black, white, and color ratios.
caustica.options.rt.purkinje.tooltip: How the eye reads color in dim light: as it adapts to darkness, sensitivity moves away from red, so red flowers, brick and torchlight fall toward black while blue, cyan and green keep their brightness. Nothing happens while the scene is bright - it starts only below roughly 5 nits of absolute scene brightness and is complete by 0.005 nits, so full daylight and dusk look exactly as they did. Needs Auto Exposure: it adapts to how bright the world actually is, not to how bright the frame was made to look.
caustica.options.rt.purkinjeStrength.too: How far the shift goes. 1.00 is the standard night-vision response; lower keeps reds readable at night, higher collapses them sooner. Mid-grey keeps its exact brightness at any value, so this changes which colors win in the dark without changing how bright the dark is.
caustica.options.rt.look.tooltip: Apply the look package's scene-referred LMT, with Advanced Color Grading off. Turn off to see the exposed image straight through ACES 2.0 - useful when telling whether a flat or lifted image comes from the look or from the lighting.
caustica.options.rt.agxExposure.tooltip: Brightness of the AgX grading, which anchors middle grey at a fixed level independent of the exposure above. Raise it with Advanced Color Grading on if the image reads dark at the same Exposure EV.
caustica.options.rt.agxSaturation.toolti: Color intensity of the AgX grading, around the image's own brightness. AgX compresses chroma hard as highlights roll off, so values above 1.00 restore the vividness that costs it. 1.00 is neutral.
caustica.options.rt.agxContrast.tooltip: Strength of the AgX contrast curve, applied where AgX works in stops. 100% is the published curve; 0% flattens it into a plain linear render with mid grey untouched; higher values darken shadows and steepen the highlight roll-off for a punchier image. Applies with Advanced Color Grading on.
caustica.options.rt.agxRange.tooltip: How many stops of scene brightness the AgX grading encodes around mid grey. Wider spends more of the curve on the highlights, so bright skies roll off more gently and the image reads flatter; narrower compresses the same scene into fewer stops for more contrast but harder clipping.
caustica.options.rt.bloomStrength.toolti: Runtime multiplier on the look package's bloom: the blurred glow bright lights add to the image before tonemapping. 100% keeps the authored strength, 0% removes it entirely.
caustica.options.rt.lensResolution.toolt: How much smaller than the screen the lens chain renders: the two flare textures are the display size divided by this, so the texel count falls with its square. 1/4 is the default and gives rings and rays their finest detail at sixteen times the cost of 1/16; coarser steps trade that faceting for fill cost.
caustica.options.rt.lensSampleRate.toolt: Multiplier on the taps both gathers take, i.e. the starburst samples and the halo samples at once. 200% is the default and doubles each per-artifact count; lower is the cheap way out when a coarse flare resolution leaves the rings faceted, higher smooths them further at a proportional cost.
caustica.options.rt.lensStarburstEnabled: Diffraction spikes from the aperture's blades, one ray pair per blade. Off keeps the halos and the dust, and skips the source reduction entirely when the halos are off too.
caustica.options.rt.lens.tooltip: Draw the light the lens itself scatters: starburst spikes from the aperture blades, halos around bright sources, and the out-of-focus dust on the front element. All three come from one chain of two low-resolution passes fed by the brightest parts of the frame, so it is cheap enough to leave on. Turn it off to compare against the same image without any lens artifacts, which also skips both passes.
caustica.options.rt.lensStarburst.toolti: How much of the radiating spike pattern each source throws. The spikes are the diffraction the aperture blades add, so their number and angle matter more than their strength: 100% is clearly visible around the sun and lamps without veiling the scene, 0% keeps the halos and dirt but drops the spikes entirely.
caustica.options.rt.lensSpikes.tooltip: The number of spike pairs radiating from each source, i.e. the aperture blade count. Odd counts give the familiar six- or eight-pointed star; low counts read as a dramatic anamorphic streak and high counts as a fine sunstar.
caustica.options.rt.lensSpikeLength.tool: How far the spikes reach from the source, as a percent of the default look (100%). Long spikes reach across the frame on a bright sun; short ones keep the star tight to the source.
caustica.options.rt.lensHaloEnabled.tool: Rings the aperture throws back at a radius that depends on wavelength, so the fringe runs blue inside and orange outside. Off keeps the starburst and the dust.
caustica.options.rt.lensHalo.tooltip: How bright the ring of light around each source is. 100% is a visible ring on the sun and strong lamps, 0% removes the rings while keeping the starburst and the dirt.
caustica.options.rt.lensHaloRadius.toolt: The ring radius as a percent of the default look (100%). The three colour copies of the ring are drawn at this radius, so a wider ring also pushes the chromatic fringe further from the source.
caustica.options.rt.lensDispersion.toolt: How far the red and blue ring copies are pushed apart, which is what turns a plain ring into a rainbow-edged one. 100% keeps the blue inside and red outside the way glass disperses them; 0% draws all three at the same radius for a neutral ring.
caustica.options.rt.lensDirtEnabled.tool: Out-of-focus dust on the front element, lit by the bloom glow. One bloom fetch per lens texel, so it is the cheapest artifact to switch off on its own.
caustica.options.rt.lensDirt.tooltip: Strength of the dust and smudges on the front element, which light up only where the scene is bright behind them. 100% shows specks and a faint grime structure over the lit part of the frame, 0% removes them.
caustica.options.rt.lensDirtScale.toolti: Size of the dust specks as a percent of the default look (100%). Higher values grow the specks into larger smudges, lower values give a fine mist of small ones.
caustica.options.rt.lensSamples.tooltip: Taps taken along each spike. Each tap is a fetch from the half-resolution source field, so this is the main cost of the starburst; too few leaves the spikes dotted instead of continuous, and beyond the point where the taps overlap the extra taps only smooth them.
caustica.options.rt.lensHaloTaps.tooltip: Taps taken around each halo ring, per colour channel. Lower values are cheaper and give a soft uneven ring; higher values make the ring a clean thin circle.
caustica.options.rt.dofMode.tooltip: Puts a lens on the camera instead of a pinhole: only the focal plane keeps its edges and everything else spreads over a blur disc. Traced samples a real aperture point per ray, so the light is defocused on the way in - a reflection, a pane of glass or a shaft of fog blurs exactly as much as whatever it came through - and the softness is assembled by the denoiser out of the frames it accumulates, settling after about a second of standing still. Post leaves the trace alone and defocuses the finished image from the depth the tracer measured, so it costs almost no frame time, needs no denoiser, and works without DLSS-RR, at the price of approximating what passed through the aperture instead of tracing it.
caustica.options.rt.dofAutoFocus.tooltip: Put the focal plane on whatever the middle of the frame is actually showing. The meter reads the depth of the surfaces the ray tracer drew, so an entity, a painting, a water face or the recessed side of a carved block focuses the frame the way it fills it, and the plane glides to wherever that lands rather than jumping. Off uses the fixed Focus Distance instead.
caustica.options.rt.dofReflectionFocus.t: Put the focal plane on what a reflection is showing rather than on the surface that carries it. A flat reflector images the thing it reflects as far behind itself as that thing stands in front, so water three blocks out holding a mountain six blocks behind it is showing something nine blocks away, and the water is not the thing your eye goes to. On, a pixel whose mirror lobe is a real share of the light it sends back — a metal, a grazing water face, a polished floor seen edge-on — reports the reflected image's distance, so the plane racks onto the mountain in the lake and the surface it appears in goes soft; a mirror carrying only sky focuses at the far stop. The distance comes from the same mirror ray the specular guides already trace, so nothing extra is rendered. Only Focus on View Centre reads it — a manual focus is a distance you dial — and off restores a meter that measures each pixel's own surface.
caustica.options.rt.dofFocusDistance.too: How far down the view axis the sharp plane sits, dialled in tenths of a block. The plane is parallel to the frame rather than a sphere around the eye, which is what a lens actually focuses. Focusing further out sharpens the horizon and leaves the foreground just as soft; focusing close is what throws the distance away.
caustica.options.rt.dofFocusTime.tooltip: How long the focal plane takes to reach a new focus: the pull is timed to have arrived once this many seconds have passed, with 99% of the defocus it had left covered. It measures that defocus in dioptres — what a surface is actually blurred by — so the plane starts moving on the first frame and only ever slows down, and a nearer surface and a further one take the same time. The target moves whenever the centre of the view finds a different surface, so a walk past a fence would fire the plane at every post; this dial decides whether the room snaps to the new depth or eases into it. The first frame after the feature is switched on starts at the target rather than gliding in.
caustica.options.rt.dofAperture.tooltip: How wide the lens opens, in centimetres - a block is a metre here, so 2 cm is a normal camera and 10 cm is an unreasonable one. A surface spreads over a disc as wide, seen from the eye, as the opening is relative to its distance, so this one dial sets how much of the frame loses its edges: 0 is a pinhole camera and everything is equally sharp. The Cap Blur Radius dials beside it then hold the frame inside one widest-possible disc, because a disc wider than one aperture point per frame can fill comes back from the denoiser as a mosaic instead of a softness.
caustica.options.rt.dofBlurCap.tooltip: Hold the frame's blur inside a widest-possible disc, however wide the Aperture asks for one. On is the denoiser-friendly camera: a disc is capped where one aperture point per frame stops being enough to fill it, which is what turns a close wall into blocks of colour instead of a softness. Off is the physically correct lens, where a surface half a block from the eye dissolves completely and the horizon softens without limit as the focal plane comes close to you. The dial beside it sets how wide the cap allows, and Cap Each Pixel decides whether it is applied to every pixel or only to the far field.
caustica.options.rt.dofMaxBlur.tooltip: The widest blur disc any layer is allowed, in pixels of the finished frame. The lens radius is narrowed per pixel against what that pixel was showing last frame to hold to it, so lowering this trades blur for cleanliness rather than moving the focal plane: 14 keeps a 4 cm lens able to throw a foreground away without ever dissolving into mosaic, 4 leaves the frame nearly sharp with only the focal plane's own edge soft, and 48 is close to switching the cap off.
caustica.options.rt.dofPerPixelCap.toolt: Apply the Max Blur Radius to every pixel against the surface it was showing last frame, not just to the horizon. On is what keeps a wall half a block from the eye a softness instead of blocks of colour, since its disc wants to be a hundred pixels wide and one aperture point per frame cannot fill that. Off holds only the far field, which the focus distance alone sets, so the foreground blurs by however wide the aperture asks - the physically correct lens, and the one the denoiser cannot resolve. Costs one render-resolution depth image read and written per frame.
caustica.options.rt.dofPinholeGuides.too: Describe the scene to DLSS-RR from the pinhole ray rather than from the aperture point this pixel happened to sample. The reconstruction assumes a pinhole camera, so guides that carry the lens sample hand it a depth, normal, albedo and mirror motion that walk across scene layers every frame, and it paints that over as a smear instead of resolving it as blur. Off saves the extra first segment - with a lens on, the primary pass walks it twice per pixel - and gives back a frame whose defocus the upscaler eats. Only matters while DLSS-RR or another reconstructing upscaler is doing the frame. Traced mode only.
caustica.options.rt.dofBlades.tooltip: The number of straight blades the post mode's opening is cut into: a point of light defocuses into a polygon with this many sides instead of a circle, the way a stopped-down camera lens draws its bokeh. 0 is a circular opening. The polygon is balanced to the circle's area, so the blade count changes the shape of the blur without changing its brightness. Post mode only.
caustica.options.rt.dofBladeRotation.too: Which way the post mode's aperture polygon faces, in degrees - visible only where a bokeh shape is bright enough to read, and only with Aperture Blades at 3 or more. Post mode only.
caustica.options.rt.dofCatEye.tooltip: How much the lens barrel clips the aperture toward the frame's edges: off-axis, the entrance pupil is the aperture and the barrel's opening drawn over each other, the opening shifted toward the frame's centre, so a highlight keeps its round side facing the centre while its outer side is bitten into - the cat-eye's crescent a real wide-open lens puts on edge and corner highlights. The corner of the frame is eclipsed hardest, and either lens renormalises what the clip leaves, so the frame does not darken. 0 keeps the opening the same shape everywhere. Both lens modes.
caustica.options.rt.dofSwirl.tooltip: How strongly field astigmatism stretches bokeh tangentially around the frame's centre: a point of light away from the axis defocuses into an ellipse whose long axis follows the circle around the centre, so a field of highlights reads as the swirl of a Petzval-type lens. It grows with the square of the field angle, so the centre stays round and the corners stretch hardest. Only the shape changes, not the brightness. 0 keeps every highlight circular. Both lens modes.
caustica.options.rt.sharpen.tooltip: Adds back the fine detail the DLSS-RR upscale averages away, applied to the finished image after tonemapping. Turn off to compare against the reconstruction exactly as the upscaler produced it.
caustica.options.rt.sharpenAmount.toolti: How much of the sharpened detail is added back. 100% is a plain unsharp mask over a 3x3 texel neighbourhood; higher values crisp up texture and thin geometry further but can ring on high-contrast edges.
caustica.options.rt.risCandidates.toolti: Candidates each surface tests when picking a glowing block to sample. Higher is less noisy on torch and lava light but costs more. Off falls back to lighting from emitters only when a ray hits one.
caustica.options.rt.spp.tooltip: Path-tracing samples taken per pixel each frame. Higher is cleaner but more demanding.
caustica.options.rt.maxBounces.tooltip: Maximum number of secondary path-tracing bounces after the primary hit. Higher captures more indirect light but costs more.
caustica.options.rt.entities.tooltip: Include entities and block entities in the ray-traced scene.
caustica.options.rt.traceSelf.tooltip: Show your own body in reflections, shadows and indirect light while in first person (you see yourself in water as others see you). Turn off to exclude your body from every ray; third person and other players are unaffected.
caustica.options.rt.particles.tooltip: Draw particles as camera-ray billboards inside the traced scene.
caustica.options.rt.glow.tooltip: Draw the vanilla Glowing-effect outline (through walls) around glowing entities.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaves.tooltip: Animate water-surface normals for moving wave highlights.
caustica.options.rt.vanillaSun.tooltip: Draw the sun from the sun sprite, so a resource pack's own art shows. Off draws it as a circular disc instead, at the same angular size the sunlight is sampled at, which makes its apparent size and the softness of its shadows agree.
caustica.options.rt.vanillaMoon.tooltip: Draw the moon from the phase sprite, so a resource pack's own art shows. Off draws a sphere lit by the sun's actual direction, so the terminator points the right way for the time of night and the surface keeps its maria.
caustica.options.rt.rainSkyDarkening.too: How much rain and thunder dim the sky and the light it delivers. At 100% each weather level removes up to 5/16 of the sky light and of everything the sky lights, the curve vanilla's own lightmap follows with its 20% floor, and the frame is then presented at that same darker level, because auto-exposure would otherwise renormalise a uniform dim straight back to where it started. 0% leaves the atmosphere clear and the exposure untouched above a storm. Clouds have their own rain response, so this dial is what closes the light down when the cloud layer is off or hidden.
caustica.options.rt.rainStreaks.tooltip: Draw falling rain while it rains. Vanilla's own weather rendering is cancelled along with the rest of its rain, so without this a storm darkens, wets and puddles the world with nothing visibly falling. Drawn after the denoiser and before the tone curve, so each streak is lit by the sky overhead and takes the same weather dimming as everything else. Snow is not drawn: the streaks are falling water, not flakes. Nothing is drawn where the biome has no liquid precipitation (a desert) or where the eye is under a roof, and the Nether and the End have no weather at all.
caustica.options.rt.rainStreakDensity.to: How many drops fall at full rain, over a fixed disc about 22 blocks across around the player. The disc keeps its size whatever the count, so a low setting is sparse rain in the same volume rather than rain confined to a smaller one, and a heavy storm is the same field filled in. Each drop is one quad built on the GPU, so this is the cheapest quality dial on the page.
caustica.options.rt.rainStreakLength.too: How long each streak is drawn, as a percent of the default look. A streak is the motion blur a falling drop leaves across one frame, so longer streaks read as heavier, faster rain and short ones as a drizzle; the speed the drops actually travel at is fixed. Longest only means most dramatic: the count and the brightness are what decide how much rain there is.
caustica.options.rt.rainStreakWidth.tool: How wide each streak is drawn, in centimetres. A drop is a couple of pixels wide at any distance you can see it, so this reads as the thickness of the near field; streaks narrower than a pixel fade out by their own coverage instead of shimmering. Wider is more like a downpour seen through a window, narrower is a fine drizzle.
How fast the rain is blown sideways, in blocks per second. The streaks lean along the wind and the drops drift with it, so one dial tilts the rain and moves it, and 0 is a vertical fall. A few blocks per second is a breeze; the default leans the streaks by about ten degrees.
Which way the rain is blown, in degrees: 0 blows toward east (+X). It uses the same compass as the cloud and fog wind, so one direction describes the whole sky, and it only means anything while the wind speed is above 0.
caustica.options.rt.rainStreakBrightness: How strongly the streaks read against the scene. They are lit by the sky directly overhead, so the rain is brightest at noon and nearly disappears into an overcast night; this dial is what makes that light visible at all. 0% keeps the storm, its darkening and its wet surfaces but draws no streaks, which is also the quickest way to tell what the pass costs.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaveHeight.tool: How tall the waves are, as a percent of the default look (100%). Taller waves break up reflections more and focus underwater caustics more sharply; 0% leaves the surface a flat mirror.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaveSize.toolti: Wavelength as a percent of the default look (100%). The whole spectrum scales together, so low values are pond ripples and high values are long ocean swell.
caustica.options.rt.waterWaveSpeed.toolt: How fast the waves travel, as a percent of the default look (100%). Long swell still moves faster than short chop at any setting; 0% freezes the surface.
caustica.options.rt.waterReflection.tool: How much of its mirror-like sky reflection the water surface keeps. At 100% water is a perfect dielectric and reproduces the bright band of sky at the horizon almost exactly, which washes the distant sea white. Lower values pass the difference into the water, where it is absorbed, so the surface darkens by taking in more light rather than by light going missing.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxDepth.toolti: How far a material's height map may sink its surface, as a percent of the depth LabPBR authors (25% of a block at 100%). Only surfaces whose normal map carries a height field are affected. Set to 0% to turn parallax off entirely and compare, which is the quickest way to tell a parallax artifact from anything else on the surface.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxLayers.toolt: Ceiling on how many height samples one displaced texel may cost. The march works out how many it needs from how far the surface has to travel, so most views pay far less than this; the ceiling only bites on steep, deep relief, where a higher one resolves the step instead of coarsening it. Lower it if parallax costs more frame time than it is worth.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxStyle.toolti: How a displaced texel is placed. Sharp snaps the displacement onto the texel grid and turns the band a step exposes into a wall, so authored hard edges — plank grooves, brick bevels, cut stone — read as cut geometry. Smooth keeps the displacement continuous and reads the height field a mip coarser, so the same relief reads as a rounded bevel carried by the material's normal map; detail thinner than that mip stops displacing at all.
caustica.options.rt.parallaxShadow.toolt: Shadow a surface with its own relief: every displaced texel walks toward the sun through the same height field, so a groove the light cannot reach into darkens. It reaches only as deep as the height the pack authored (a quarter block at most), so it reads as contact shading inside the relief rather than as a shadow cast across the face. Costs another pass of height samples on displaced texels only; switch it off to measure that.
caustica.options.rt.entityParallax.toolt: Run the height-field parallax march on entities as well as on terrain. Entities only carry a height field when a resource pack gives them a normal map with an authored alpha, so with vanilla assets this changes nothing.
caustica.options.rt.textureEmission.tool: Honour the emissive channel a resource pack authors in its own specular map. It is the only light a material's textures can add by themselves; switching it off leaves the rest of the material intact and is the way to tell whether a glow belongs to the texture or to the block.
caustica.options.rt.blockEmission.toolti: Honour light emitted by the block itself rather than by its texture: glowing block states such as glowstone, lava, torches and the like. Light already published to the emitter list keeps lighting the room until that section is rebuilt, so give it a moment after switching.
caustica.options.rt.subsurface.tooltip: Honour the subsurface scattering a material's LabPBR map asks for, which lets light bleed a short distance through waxy and organic surfaces. Switched off, those surfaces keep their colour and shading but stop scattering.
caustica.options.rt.porosity.tooltip: Honour the porosity a material's LabPBR map asks for, which is what lets a wet surface absorb water and darken. Switched off, Surface Wetness still adds its sheen but nothing drinks it, which separates a wet world from a porous material.
caustica.options.rt.wetness.tooltip: How much water the world has, against the porosity each material's own LabPBR map was authored with. At 0% everything is dry and porous surfaces look exactly as authored; at 100% a porous surface darkens and turns reflective as far as its map allows, so sand and wool react strongly while metal and glass stay unchanged. This sets how wet the world is, not which materials are porous.
caustica.options.rt.rainWetness.tooltip: How much rain soaks into every surface on top of Surface Wetness. The soak builds while it rains and dries slowly after it stops, so stone and soil stay dark and reflective through a gap in the shower instead of snapping back. At 0% rain leaves the world as dry as the Surface Wetness slider says. Deserts, the Nether and the End receive no weather, so their ground stays dry.
caustica.options.rt.puddleCoverage.toolt: How much level, upward-facing ground collects standing water once the world is soaked. A puddle is a near-mirror film: it flattens the normal map, drops roughness to the water's own value and returns the water's Fresnel, so it reflects the sky and the world instead of just looking polished. 0% keeps surfaces wet but never pooled. Only liquid rain pools: snow, deserts, the Nether and the End never collect standing water.
caustica.options.rt.fog.tooltip: Rayleigh aerial perspective integrated inside the path tracer: the air scatters blue far more than red, so distant terrain fades and blues out while the low sun reddens through it, and the fog's own light follows the sky. Off by default.
caustica.options.rt.fogDensity.tooltip: Rayleigh density at the fog base, in 1/block. The air's per-channel coefficient turns it into an extinction, so it fades blue about four times faster than red: at the default 0.0005 blue light is cut to 1/e at 4 km and red at 51 km, the scale of a clear day. Higher values close in until only tens of blocks stay visible inside the fog.
caustica.options.rt.fogDayDecay.tooltip: How much of the sunrise/sunset peak the fog loses at noon and at night. 0% (the default) holds the density constant around the clock, which is what Rayleigh air does; raise it to model a mist that belongs to the hour, up to 100% leaving fog only around sunrise and sunset.
caustica.options.rt.fogHeight.tooltip: How many blocks of altitude the fog takes to fall to 1/e of its base density. 43 thins the air by half every thirty blocks, which is the default; small values hug the ground, large ones fill valleys and climb hillsides.
caustica.options.rt.fogBaseY.tooltip: The world height where the fog's constant-density region ends and the exponential falloff begins, in absolute Y blocks. The default 93 puts its shoulder thirty blocks above sea level.
caustica.options.rt.fogAnisotropy.toolti: How strongly the fog forward-scatters light. Rayleigh air scatters symmetrically, so 0% (the default) is the physical value; positive values brighten fog in the direction of the sun or moon, which is what turns a flat bright haze into visible beams.
caustica.options.rt.fogAlbedo.tooltip: The fraction of extinguished light the fog scatters back out rather than absorbs. 100% (the default) is clear air that absorbs nothing; low values make fog darken with thickness like smoke.
caustica.options.rt.fogAmbient.tooltip: Weight of the sky's own irradiance in the fog's lighting. This is what keeps night fog from going black — it fades with the sky instead of adding a constant glow.
caustica.options.rt.fogShadow.tooltip: Casts one shadow ray per pixel toward the sun or moon so terrain, trees and buildings cut real light shafts out of the fog. Off leaves the sun term unoccluded — uniform bright fog with no god rays.
caustica.options.rt.fogShadowFloor.toolt: The density fully-shadowed fog keeps. 0% hard-culls the fog from shadow — crisp shadow volumes but sterile edges; higher values keep more milk in sealed rooms and shaded valleys. 95% nearly disables the cull.
caustica.options.rt.fogMarch.tooltip: Steps the fog integral instead of using the closed form, so the fog gathers into wind-drifted billows and every sample casts its own sun shadow ray. Costly; with noise at 0% it converges to the same result as the analytic fog.
caustica.options.rt.fogNoise.tooltip: How strongly the fog density gathers into billows around its height profile. 0% reproduces the smooth analytic fog exactly; higher values make clumpy, uneven fog.
caustica.options.rt.fogWindSpeed.tooltip: How fast the billow field drifts, in blocks per second. The drift is a smooth translation of a world-anchored field, so shapes move steadily instead of boiling per frame.
caustica.options.rt.fogWindAngle.tooltip: The compass direction the billow field drifts toward. 0° blows toward +X (east).
caustica.options.rt.fogMarchSteps.toolti: March samples per path segment. More steps resolve the billows and light shafts more exactly but cost proportionally more; 16 is balanced, 64 is the convergence reference.
caustica.options.rt.fogJitter.tooltip: Scatters each march sample inside its step with a stable blue-noise pattern. 0% bands visibly at step edges; 100% dithers them into a grain the denoiser resolves into soft edges.
caustica.options.rt.cloudCoverage.toolti: Threshold the shape field must clear, 0–200%. 70% is nearly clear, 100% is broken cumulus with blue sky between the heaps, 120% covers about two thirds of the sky, and 180% is a solid overcast. The two high sheets thicken with it but stay thin.
caustica.options.rt.cloudPatchiness.tool: How far the large-scale field outweighs the fine one. Low values give ragged, shredded edges spread evenly over the sky; high values gather the bodies into weather systems with large gaps between them.
caustica.options.rt.cloudAltitude.toolti: World height the cumulus decks stand on, in blocks. The towering deck and the two high sheets hang at fixed offsets above it.
caustica.options.rt.cloudThickness.toolt: Height scale of the two cumulus decks. The low deck stands 0.56 of it deep and the towering deck 1.21, so this deepens both bodies without changing their coverage, their opacity or where they sit.
caustica.options.rt.cloudSize.tooltip: Horizontal scale of the noise every deck is cut from, against an authored reference of 368 blocks. Smaller gives small puffs, larger gives broad decks; height is a separate dial.
caustica.options.rt.cloudDensity.tooltip: Multiplier on every deck's authored extinction, so it moves the body's solidity and the shadow it casts together. 100% is the authored table — a cumulus near 0.5 per block, a cirrus a hundred times thinner.
caustica.options.rt.cloudWindSpeed.toolt: How fast the cloud field drifts, in blocks per second. The drift is a smooth translate of a world-anchored field — clouds move, they do not boil.
caustica.options.rt.cloudWindAngle.toolt: Compass direction the cloud field drifts toward. 0° blows toward +X (east).
caustica.options.rt.cloudFadeDistance.to: Distance in blocks where the cumulus decks fully dissipate: nothing renders past it, and the fade begins at 60% of this range. The two high sheets ride eight times this, because a sheet five kilometres up is crossed far beyond the cumulus band. Cloud shadows keep working beyond the fade — the deck still exists overhead.
caustica.options.rt.cloudVolumetric.tool: Walk through every deck the ray meets instead of crossing each once: real vertical structure, parallax as the camera moves, and a lit crown over a dark underbelly. Pays a step budget per primary-ray pixel; reflections and bounces keep the cheap mean extinction, so what they see is dimmed but not re-lit.
caustica.options.rt.cloudSteps.tooltip: Step budget per deck that the volumetric tier walks. The two cumulus decks split it; the high sheets are five blocks deep and take a crossing each. Cost is linear in this, and the dithering the denoiser has to resolve is inversely so.
caustica.options.rt.cloudLightSteps.tool: Samples the sun leg takes through its own deck per volumetric cloud sample. 1 is the single midpoint tap the tier shipped with; more resolve the light gradient through a body — a crown shadowing its own base. Cost is linear in this, on top of the march budget.
caustica.options.rt.cloudDetail.tooltip: The erosion cut that bites a close cumulus silhouette and the curl that breaks a cirrus sheet into filaments. Off reads the shape the ground shadow field and the light legs already use - a cumulus un-eroded, a sheet unwarped - several texture fetches cheaper per march sample. A deck keeps its coverage, crown and base, and the shadow it casts, either way.
caustica.options.rt.cloudShadowSteps.too: Samples the ground shadow field takes through each deck along the sun leg. 1 prices the whole slab at its mid-plane crossing; more resolve a broken deck's shadow gaps and a thick deck's dark core. Every sun-lit surface, fog leg and shaft reads this field, so the cost spreads across the whole frame.
caustica.options.rt.cloudRainBoost.toolt: How much rain and thunder thicken the sky. Rain raises every cumulus deck's coverage threshold — the deck closes by the bodies growing into each other — and multiplies the density, so shadows go storm-dark; thunder adds a third again. 0% holds the sky to the sliders whatever the weather.
caustica.options.rt.cloudFlow.tooltip: How fast each deck's fine detail scrolls against its body. The wind moves the whole field; this moves only the detail inside it, so edges undulate and interiors billow instead of the sky sliding rigidly. 0% freezes the shapes and leaves only the wind's drift.
caustica.options.rt.volumeQuality.toolti: Sets the whole volumetric system at once and WRITES the settings on the Volumetrics and Sky pages, so what those controls show is what the frame is doing. Off clears every one of them and renders the world exactly as it did before the system existed; each tier above it adds one effect: Low the clouds and the water fog, Medium the volumetric deck, High the fog layer, Ultra the marched fog. The name is a reading of those switches, not a memory: change one by hand and this row says Custom until they spell a tier again, and the shipped defaults are one such mix, so a fresh install starts there.
caustica.options.rt.cloud.tooltip: Four procedural decks over the world — a low cumulus layer, a towering one above it, an altostratus sheet and a cirrus sheet — plus the shadows they cast on terrain, fog and water. Renders only where the sky lights the world; off keeps the sky exactly as before.
caustica.options.rt.cloudShadow.tooltip: Dim the sun wherever the deck stands between it and the world. Terrain, fog, water and shafts read the same shadow field, so a clouded sun loses its light everywhere at once. Off leaves the visible clouds unchanged and lights the world as if the sky were clear.
caustica.options.rt.fogRainBoost.tooltip: How strongly rain thickens the fog: density scales by 100% + boost × rain level, on top of the day curve rather than replacing it. 0% keeps the fog weather-blind.
caustica.options.rt.boundaryFog.tooltip: The air closes in as you approach a world border. It joins the volumetric fog's own medium, so it scatters the sun and the sky like fog does and keeps working with Volumetric Fog off. Nothing happens until you come within the band below of a border, which is the ordinary case: a default world border sits about 30 million blocks out, so this needs a shrunk one (/worldborder set 200). Costs one multiply-add per fog sample — it adds no rays and no pass.
caustica.options.rt.boundaryFogDensity.t: How thick the air is at the border itself, in the same units as Fog Density: 6% leaves about 17 blocks of visibility at the wall. It falls to nothing across the band below, and the falloff is squared, so most of the band stays nearly clear and the veil announces itself instead of dimming the whole world.
caustica.options.rt.boundaryFogRamp.tool: How far from a world border the haze begins, in blocks. At the border the density is full; walk out past this distance and it is gone. It is measured from where you stand, not from what you look at, so the whole view veils together — the same shape vanilla's border fog had. A wider band starts the veil earlier; it does not cost more.
caustica.options.rt.edgeFade.tooltip: Dissolves the hard stepped cliff where the loaded world stops. This is a fade, not a fog: nothing is added to the air and no light is scattered, so the mid distance keeps its contrast and colour — distant terrain simply gives way to the sky it was standing against, and the cut edge goes. It is measured from the eye, so a mirror or a pane of glass showing the far side of the world carries the same fade the direct view does. Costs no extra rays and no extra pass, and it works with volumetric fog off.
caustica.options.rt.edgeFadeOpacity.tool: How much of the farthest visible terrain has dissolved by the time the view reaches the render edge. 90% leaves a tenth of the surface showing; 100% removes the boundary completely. The fade ramps smoothly up to this value from Edge Fade Start, so the same setting looks the same at 4 chunks and at 32.
caustica.options.rt.edgeFadeStart.toolti: How much of the view distance stays untouched: the fade begins at this fraction of the way out and climbs across the rest. 50% keeps the near half of the view fully solid. Lower values begin the dissolve closer to you and thin more of the scene; 0% starts at the eye, which reads as a general loss of contact shadow at range rather than as an edge treatment.
caustica.options.rt.shafts.tooltip: Tyndall rays: sunlight scattering in whatever medium the view passes through, independent of volumetric fog. Eight ray-traced sun-visibility probes per pixel trace where the shadow volumes are, and the light is only drawn where the view crosses one — a path that stays in the sun carries no beam, which is what keeps the effect from reading as a haze over the whole frame. In air this is the beams through windows, leaves and cave mouths, with the fog off and the scene still crisp. Underwater the same integrator runs on the water body's own scattering, so the shafts follow the water's extinction and pick up the wave focus where the sunlight crosses the surface; water with no scattering setting has nothing to light.
caustica.options.rt.shaftIntensity.toolt: Overall strength of the beams, 100% being the physical single scatter of the medium below. This is the cheap knob: it changes no sample count, so raise it instead of the density when the beams are too faint.
caustica.options.rt.shaftDensity.tooltip: Extinction of the air the shafts scatter in, in 1/block. It sets how quickly a beam fades with distance: at the default 0.0055 a 30-block beam carries about 15% of the medium and a 192-block one about 65%, while 0.03 spends a beam inside 35 blocks. Raising it shortens the beams rather than brightening them — use intensity for brightness.
caustica.options.rt.shaftAnisotropy.tool: How strongly the airborne light favours the direction of the sun. This is what turns lit haze into a beam: 0% (the default) is a flat glow in every direction, 70% gives the long visible rays, and past 90% the beams collapse into a halo around the sun and disappear from the shade they should cross.
caustica.options.rt.shaftDistance.toolti: How far from the camera the beams are integrated, in blocks. Shorter keeps the shafts local to the trees and walls in front of you; longer carries them across a valley. Costs the same per pixel either way — this is a look control, not a quality one.
caustica.options.rt.waterShaftDensity.to: Extinction of the water the underwater beams scatter in, in 1/block; 0 (the default) removes them. This is a medium of its own rather than a property of the water body, so the beams can be lit without changing how opaque the water is. 0.03 puts the e-folding at 33 blocks, which is roughly the visibility a murky column has anyway.
caustica.options.rt.waterShaftCeiling.to: How much brighter the sun's own direction may make the water than the rest of the column. It is the control that keeps the surface you look up at from turning white: the forward lobe peaks far above its surroundings and the path to the surface is long, so without a ceiling the beams arrive an order of magnitude over the water they sit in. Lower gives more directional beams; higher gives a brighter, softer body of water.
caustica.options.rt.waterFog.tooltip: The water body’s own haze: what a submerged view sees between itself and whatever it is looking at. It is lit by the sky above the surface and by the sun, and it fades with depth because the light has to reach it through the water. Off leaves the body purely absorbing, so the water only darkens with distance.
caustica.options.rt.waterFogDensity.tool: How much of the light the water swallows it scatters back instead of absorbing, as a share of the water’s own extinction. 15% is the default haze; higher values make the body glow and hide what is behind it, 0% is clear water. Because it is a share of the extinction it can never out-brighten the light the water took away, and murkier water (Water Opacity) scatters more at the same share.
caustica.options.rt.waterFogAnisotropy.t: How strongly the water’s haze throws light forward. 0% scatters evenly, which reads as flat murk; higher values brighten the sun’s own direction and let a beam read through the surface. 60% is the default sea-water value.
caustica.options.rt.waterFogAmbient.tool: Weight on the sky’s light inside the water haze, as a share of the irradiance the surface lets through. Underwater light is mostly the sky’s, so this is what decides how lit the body reads; 0% leaves only the sun’s own lobe.
caustica.options.rt.waterOpacity.tooltip: How strongly water absorbs light, relative to the default murk (3x). Water swallows red about four times faster than blue, so a body turns teal with depth; lower values make it clearer so you can see the bottom, higher values make it murkier and darker. 0 removes absorption entirely.
caustica.options.rt.hdr.tooltip: Recreate the swapchain for HDR (ST.2084/PQ) or native SDR output. Applied at the next frame boundary.
caustica.options.rt.hdrUiBrightness.tool: Absolute brightness (in nits) assigned to SDR-authored UI on an HDR display.
caustica.options.rt.hdrPeak.tooltip: Absolute brightness (in nits) highlights roll off toward. Set to your display's peak HDR brightness.
caustica.options.rt.dlssQuality.tooltip: DLSS Ray Reconstruction quality mode. Lower-quality modes render fewer pixels and upscale more aggressively for higher framerates; higher-quality modes render more pixels for a sharper image. Only affects the image when DLSS Ray Reconstruction is enabled.
caustica.options.rt.debugView.tooltip: Inspect ray-tracing buffers and exposure diagnostics after the normal frame has rendered.
caustica.setting.enabled.tooltip: Trace the scene with hardware ray tracing instead of the built-in rasterizer. The Ray Tracing key binding (Controls, Caustica category) flips the same switch in-game.
caustica.setting.worker-threads.tooltip: Background threads that build and upload terrain acceleration structures. More loads terrain faster but takes more CPU time. Applied at startup, so it needs a game restart.
caustica.setting.asyncDispatch.tooltip: How many terrain sections are submitted for building in one render pass. Higher loads terrain faster but uses more CPU and GPU time.
caustica.setting.completionResults.toolt: How many finished terrain builds are collected in one render pass. Higher commits terrain sooner but uses more time per pass.
caustica.setting.maxInflight.tooltip: How many terrain sections may be building at the same time.
caustica.setting.sectionTableCapacity.to: Starting size of the table that holds one acceleration structure per terrain section.
caustica.setting.rebaseDistance.tooltip: Distance, in blocks, after which terrain coordinates are re-anchored around the camera so float precision stays fine far from the origin.
caustica.setting.blasCompaction.tooltip: Shrink rebuilt terrain acceleration structures after building them.
caustica.setting.minFillRatio.tooltip: How much of a block a glowing block has to fill before it is treated as an area emitter rather than a point light.
caustica.setting.lightTemporalReuse.tool: Carry each pixel's chosen emitter light forward from the previous frame and keep averaging it, instead of re-picking from scratch every frame. Turn off to compare the two directly at one spot.
caustica.setting.lightTemporalHistory.to: How many effective samples a pixel's emitter choice may accumulate before it stops admitting older frames. Lower keeps more per-frame randomness, which the upscaler averages instead of the reservoir; higher converges the brightness but freezes which emitter the pixel is lit by.
caustica.setting.lightStats.tooltip: Log the size of the ray-traced emitter hierarchy — how many emitters, section slots and grid spans it holds, how much memory that takes, and how many emitter indices survive each rebuild — every time it is rebuilt.
caustica.setting.lightDump.tooltip: Log one line per ray-traced emitter near the player each time the hierarchy is rebuilt, with its world position, area and emitted light, followed by a count.
caustica.setting.lightDumpRadius.tooltip: How far around the player, in blocks, the emitter dump reaches.
caustica.setting.nameTags.tooltip: Draw entity name tags inside the traced scene instead of over it.
caustica.setting.entityRefit.tooltip: Update a moving entity's acceleration structure in place instead of rebuilding it.
caustica.setting.maxOrdinary.tooltip: Upper bound on how many ordinary entities are captured into the traced scene. Needs a game restart.
caustica.setting.maxBlockEntities.toolti: Upper bound on how many block entities, such as signs and chests, are captured into the traced scene. Needs a game restart.
caustica.setting.beViewChunks.tooltip: How many chunks around the camera are searched for block entities to capture.
caustica.setting.beBuilds.tooltip: How many block entity renderers are captured in one frame. Higher fills the scene sooner but costs more per frame.
caustica.setting.maxEntityTextures.toolt: How many distinct entity textures are held open at once. Needs a game restart.
caustica.setting.entityPbr.tooltip: Read LabPBR material maps for entities so they can be rough, metallic, or emissive. Needs a game restart.
caustica.setting.captureParity.tooltip: Debug only: capture every entity model twice and require the two results to match exactly. Halves entity capture speed.
caustica.setting.maxParticles.tooltip: Upper bound on how many particles are captured into the traced scene. Needs a game restart.
caustica.setting.blockOutline.tooltip: Draw the targeted-block outline inside the traced scene instead of over it.
caustica.setting.exposureKey.tooltip: The scene brightness auto exposure treats as middle grey. Raising it brightens everything the meter sees; it does not change how much the meter compensates for scene range.
caustica.setting.adaptDarken.tooltip: Seconds auto exposure takes to adjust when the scene gets darker, such as walking into a cave.
caustica.setting.adaptBrighten.tooltip: Seconds auto exposure takes to adjust when the scene gets brighter, such as stepping back outside.
caustica.setting.lowPercentile.tooltip: The lower edge of the measured luminance range that auto exposure keeps.
caustica.setting.highPercentile.tooltip: The upper edge of the measured luminance range that auto exposure keeps.
caustica.setting.exposureStride.tooltip: How many pixels are skipped when sampling the frame for exposure. Higher meters faster and less accurately.
caustica.setting.centerSigma.tooltip: How wide the region at the middle of the screen is that counts more heavily toward exposure.
caustica.setting.centerFloor.tooltip: How much weight the rest of the screen keeps next to the centre region.
caustica.setting.skyWeightCap.tooltip: Limits how much open sky can pull on exposure, so looking at the horizon does not darken the ground.
caustica.setting.emissiveWeightCap.toolt: Limits how much glowing blocks can pull on exposure, so a torch in view does not darken the room.
caustica.setting.preExposure.tooltip: Store the traced image at the previous frame's exposure scale and divide it back out when displaying, so values stay near middle grey instead of spanning the full photometric range. Cancels exactly, so toggling it should not change the image; it exists to check that, and as an escape hatch if the upscaler proves sensitive to its history scale.
caustica.setting.dlssRr.tooltip: Denoise the traced image with NVIDIA Ray Reconstruction instead of presenting it directly. Requires supported hardware and drivers.
caustica.setting.dlssRrFireflyClamp.tool: Cap isolated single-texel spikes in the traced frame before Ray Reconstruction sees it. Off hands the trace over untouched.
caustica.setting.shadowSkipDepth.tooltip: Stops tracing the emitter shadow ray at vertices deeper than this many bounces and treats them as unoccluded. 0 keeps every shadow in the indirect light; 1 drops the ray for every bounce after the first, which is the fastest setting at the cost of light leaking into far-bounce corners.
caustica.setting.indirectSubsample.toolt: Traces the indirect lighting for two of every three pixels and rebuilds the rest from a depth-aware upsample. Saves about a fifth of the indirect ray work; the indirect light gets softer and slightly darker. Off traces every pixel.
caustica.setting.radianceCache.tooltip: Ends each indirect path at its first bounce and reads the light that would have come from beyond it out of a world-space probe grid, instead of tracing the deeper bounces. The grid is filled by the pixels on screen and by a few thousand probe rays per frame, so a light that changes takes a moment to reach the cache. Off traces every bounce.
caustica.setting.stillInfinite.tooltip: Keep summing until the still-render key is pressed again instead of stopping at the sample count. The screen shows the running mean, so F2 takes the accumulated picture at any moment; the stopping press resolves and saves the run as well.
caustica.setting.stillResolutionSwitch.t: Resize the window to the width and height below for the duration of a still run, then put it back when the run ends or is dropped. The render target and the saved PNG follow the window, so a picture can be accumulated larger than the desktop; a fullscreen run keeps the display's own size instead.
caustica.setting.stillWidth.tooltip: Window width a still run switches to, in screen pixels. 0 keeps the current window width.
caustica.setting.stillHeight.tooltip: Window height a still run switches to, in screen pixels. 0 keeps the current window height.
caustica.setting.stillDenoise.tooltip: Filter the accumulated mean before it is tone mapped, using the surface normal, albedo and depth the tracer already wrote. A run without DLSS-RR sums raw frames, so its mean still carries noise at about 1 over the square root of the sample count; this removes the part of it that neighbouring pixels saw from the same surface, and leaves textures, silhouettes and fine geometry alone. It cannot recover detail the sample count never reached - raising the sample count is the only thing that does. A run with DLSS-RR on is already reconstructed and skips the filter.
caustica.setting.stillDenoiseStrength.to: How much of the filter the still render's mean takes. 0% saves the raw accumulated mean, 100% the whole filtered result; halfway keeps half of each, so a texture that only exists in the noise fades instead of being erased.
caustica.setting.stillLegacyAccumulation: Sum with the earlier estimator: each sample is capped at eight times its pixel running mean, and the filter falls back to a fixed 2/sqrt(N) tolerance. Kept for reproducing earlier pictures; the cap darkens the mean and cannot remove a spike that arrives on the first sample.
caustica.setting.dlssPreset.tooltip: 0 lets the Ray Reconstruction library choose its own default for the selected quality mode. Leave at 0 unless diagnosing upscaling behaviour.
caustica.setting.frameGeneration.tooltip: Generate additional displayed frames between traced ones. Requires a supported frame-generation backend; pick it below. V-Sync must be on for the display to show them.
Which backend fills the generated frames. DLSS is NVIDIA's and needs an RTX 40-series or newer GPU and supported drivers; it can generate up to three extra frames per traced frame. FSR 3.1 is AMD's, runs on any Vulkan 1.3 device, and generates one. Self Interpolation uses this mod's own motion vectors, and Duplicate presents the traced frame twice without interpolating; both are diagnostics. Requires a game restart.
caustica.setting.multiFrameCount.tooltip: 1 displays 2 frames per traced frame, 2 displays 3, and so on. DLSS only; FSR 3.1 always generates one frame.
caustica.setting.reflex.tooltip: Reduce click-to-photon latency through the low-latency Vulkan interface. Requires supported hardware.
caustica.setting.reflexBoost.tooltip: Raise GPU clocks while frames are being rendered.
caustica.setting.reflexInterval.tooltip: Pace frames to at most one per this many microseconds. 0 leaves the rate uncontrolled.
caustica.setting.jitterSignX.tooltip: Sign applied to the horizontal part of the sub-pixel jitter, both as reported to the upscaler and as applied to primary rays. The default follows the validated DLSS convention for Vulkan's flipped clip space. Change only when diagnosing upscaling artefacts.
caustica.setting.jitterSignY.tooltip: Sign applied to the vertical part of the sub-pixel jitter, both as reported to the upscaler and as applied to primary rays. The default follows the validated DLSS convention for Vulkan's flipped clip space. Change only when diagnosing upscaling artefacts.
caustica.setting.frameStats.tooltip: Write per-frame ray-tracing counters to rt-frame-stats/frame.csv and log a line when a frame hitches.
caustica.setting.exr.tooltip: Save an ACEScg EXR beside the normal F2 PNG while ray tracing is active.
caustica.options.rt.screenshot.exrUnavai: No ray-traced frame available for a residual-exposure EXR
caustica.setting.stillSamples.tooltip: How many frames the still-render hotkey averages into one PNG. The run saves itself once it has this many, and moving the camera restarts the count. More samples is a cleaner image and a longer wait.
caustica.setting.heavyDiagnostics.toolti: Enable vendor Vulkan diagnostics and a full crash dump on device loss. Roughly ten times slower acceleration structure builds and a measurable framerate cost, so turn on only while chasing a live crash.
caustica.hotkey.rt.restart: Ray tracing: on (restart the game to apply)
caustica.hotkey.still.started.infinite: Still render: accumulating until the key is pressed again
caustica.hotkey.still.unavailable: Still render needs ray tracing in a world
caustica.hotkey.still.resolution: Still render: resizing the window to %sx%s
caustica.hotkey.still.fullscreen: Still render: leave fullscreen to use the still resolution
caustica.setting.dhLod.tooltip: Meshes Distant Horizons' far terrain as flat-colour geometry into the ray-traced scene beyond the traced world's edge, so the horizon follows DH's render distance instead of the vanilla one. Inert without the DH mod installed. DH's own rasterized LOD rendering is switched off while this is on — the ray tracer draws the far field instead.
caustica.setting.dhLodMaxDistance.toolti: How far the LOD field reaches from the player, in blocks. 0 follows Distant Horizons' own chunk render distance, so raising DH's slider extends the traced horizon with it. The outermost rings render at 64-block cells; past that more distance buys atmosphere, not detail.
caustica.setting.dhLodEmissive.tooltip: Distant caves, village windows and lava sheets glow at night: DH reports a block-light level per column, run through the same heuristic-emission curve as traced terrain. Off keeps the far field unlit by emissives, which reads slightly flatter at night.
caustica.setting.dhLodFetchBudget.toolti: Render-thread microseconds per frame spent reading DH's LOD data (the queries hit DH's cache-backed database and cannot run off-thread). Lower values spread the initial fill over more frames; raise only if the horizon grows too slowly.
